beats.text: In *1739*, a foreign king walked into *Delhi*, stayed *57 days*,
and left with so much treasure...
...that he cancelled taxes back home in *Persia* for three whole years.
Not the British. Not a Mongol. A guy most people have never heard of.
And here's the thing. That wasn't even India's *worst century*.
For most of the last thousand years, India was the *richest place on Earth*.
At one point, this one country produced about *a quarter*
of everything made on the entire planet.
About 250 years later, it produced around *four percent*.
beats.fix: Script said 'Two hundred years later ... around three percent'. Maddison: 24.4% (1700) to 4.2% (1950).

beats.text: It was *invaded*, *looted*, *split in half*, and *starved*,
and it is now the *most populated country* in the world
and one of the fastest growing economies on it.
So how does a place get robbed that many times
and keep standing back up?
To understand that, we have to go back
to a *temple on the coast* that kept getting emptied out.

sections.title: Act 1: The Richest House on the Street with No Lock on the Door

beats.text: Around the year *1000*, India was *not a country*.
Let me be clear about that, because everything else depends on it.
Look at this map. See all those separate colours?
*Hundreds of kingdoms*, dozens of languages,
and a warrior class called the *Rajputs*
who were genuinely some of the bravest fighters in the world
and absolutely could not stop fighting each other.
Rajputs had a *code of honour*. You fought fair. You gave warning.
You didn't hit a man who'd already lost.
It was beautiful, and it was about to get *very expensive*.
Because up in Afghanistan, a ruler named *Mahmud of Ghazni* had noticed something.
India's temples weren't just places of worship. *They were banks*.
Kings donated gold to them for centuries.
Solid gold statues, jewelled doors, vaults nobody had ever touched.
So Mahmud came down through the mountain passes and robbed them.
Then he did it again. Then again.
*Seventeen* separate raids over about thirty years.
His most famous target was the temple of *Somnath*
on the western coast in *1025*,
and the gold he carried out of that single building
funded an entire empire back in Afghanistan.
He never tried to stay. He just came, emptied the place, and went home.
*Seventeen times*.
Nobody stopped him, because there was no "nobody" to stop him.
There were just a hundred kings who all assumed it was somebody else's problem.
About *170 years later*, a different Afghan ruler showed up with a different plan.
His name was *Muhammad Ghori*, and he didn't want the gold.
*He wanted the land*.
He ran into the strongest king in northern India, *Prithviraj Chauhan*,
at a place called *Tarain* in *1191*. Prithviraj crushed him. Completely.
Ghori was badly wounded and only just escaped.
beats.fix: Script said Ghori was captured alive. Contemporary sources (Minhaj) say he was wounded and carried to safety; the capture-and-release is later legend.

beats.text: But according to the stories, he was captured, and Prithviraj did the honourable thing.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Sir, we've captured the invader.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Excellent. Bring him here.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: He's right here. On his knees. Weeping, actually.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Right. Let him go.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'm sorry?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: He's beaten. It's dishonourable to kill a beaten man.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: He came here specifically to take your kingdom.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: And he failed. Give him a horse.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: A horse?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: He can't walk back to Afghanistan.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Sir, what if he comes back?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Then I'll beat him again.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: ...Should I write that down somewhere?
He came back. One year later, same field,
and this time Ghori attacked at dawn before the Rajput army had formed up,
which was *not how it was supposed to be done*.
Prithviraj lost, and northern India lost with him.
Ghori went home to Afghanistan and handed his new Indian territory
to a trusted commander to run.
That commander was not a prince. He was not a noble.
He had been *bought and sold* as property.
